101.event_title: Raoul Wallenberg protects the Jews of Budapest
101.event: Swedish businessman Raoul Wallenberg, recruited by the US War Refugee Board and given diplomatic status by the Swedish legation, arrived in Budapest on 9 July 1944 and began distributing Swedish certificates of protection to Hungarian Jews. Using Swedish and War Refugee Board funds he set up hospitals, nurseries, a soup kitchen and more than 30 protected houses, and he repeatedly intervened in person to have holders of protective papers released from deportation columns. He was last seen with Soviet officials on 17 January 1945 and disappeared in Soviet custody.
101.explanation: Wallenberg had no prior tie to the people he protected and nothing to gain from them; many of those he helped never had the chance even to thank him, and his fate has never been fully explained.
101.tie_back: Help given to strangers who had done nothing to earn it, at the risk of the giver's own life, is exactly the kind of benefit the kural says earth and heaven together could not repay.
101._accuracy_note: A very close fit for unearned, unrepayable help; the kural speaks from the recipient's side, while the documented record focuses on the giver.

102.event_title: The little ships help evacuate Dunkirk
102.place: Dunkirk, France, and the English Channel
102.event: With British, French and Belgian troops trapped around the French port of Dunkirk, the Royal Navy organised Operation Dynamo to bring them back across the Channel. Because large warships could not approach the shallow beaches, the British Admiralty appealed to the owners of small boats, and these little ships, many of them requisitioned and mostly crewed by naval personnel, ferried men from the beaches to the larger vessels offshore. More than 338,000 British and French soldiers were rescued, far more than the government had first expected.
102.explanation: Many of the vessels were small pleasure craft and launches, yet arriving at the one moment when the army's survival hung in the balance made them part of a rescue that kept Britain's trained army intact.
102.tie_back: The kural says a favour done at the moment of need, however small, outweighs the world; the little ships mattered because of when they came, not because of their size.
102._accuracy_note: Timeliness fits well, but IWM notes that most soldiers actually left from the harbour mole on large ships, so the small boats were only one part of the rescue.

103.event_title: CERN puts the World Wide Web in the public domain
103.event: British scientist Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web in 1989 while working at CERN, the European particle physics laboratory, to help scientists share information. On 30 April 1993 CERN published a statement putting the World Wide Web software in the public domain, making it available royalty-free to anyone; a later release was issued under an open licence. CERN states that these actions allowed the web to flourish.
103.explanation: By declining to charge for the technology, CERN let anyone add a server, create pages or build a browser, and the web spread around the world within a few years.
103.tie_back: The kural praises help given by those who do not weigh what they will get back; releasing the web free of royalties is a gift whose value to the world is hard to measure.
103._accuracy_note: A strong example of help given without calculating returns, though it was an institutional decision partly aimed at maximising the web's spread rather than a purely personal act of kindness.

104.event_title: Gail Halvorsen, the Candy Bomber of Berlin
104.event: During the Berlin Airlift, US Air Force pilot Gail Halvorsen met children at the fence of Tempelhof airfield and shared two sticks of gum with them, then began dropping chocolate and gum tied to small handkerchief parachutes from his transport plane, at first without permission. The airlift commander, Lt. Gen. William H. Tunner, approved and expanded the drops as Operation Little Vittles, and an estimated 46,000 pounds of candy was dropped on more than 250,000 parachutes. Halvorsen later commanded the American air base at Tempelhof from 1970 to 1974, and in 1974 the West German government awarded him its Order of Merit.
104.explanation: Sweets dropped to hungry children were tiny compared with the food and coal of the airlift, yet Berliners and the wider world remembered the Candy Bomber for the rest of his life.
104.tie_back: The kural says those who understand kindness treat a millet-seed favour as if it were a palm tree; a few sweets on handkerchief parachutes were honoured by a whole nation decades later.
104._accuracy_note: Good fit for small favours magnified by grateful recipients, though the candy drops were part of a much larger relief effort.

105.event_title: Andrew Carnegie repays Colonel Anderson's library
105.place: Allegheny (now part of Pittsburgh), Pennsylvania, United States
105.event: As a poor working boy in Allegheny, Andrew Carnegie borrowed books from Colonel James Anderson, a retired businessman who opened his personal library of about 400 volumes to working boys every Saturday. Carnegie later became one of the richest men in the world, and starting in 1881 he and later his foundation gave some $56 million to build 2,509 public libraries. In 1904 a monument by the sculptor Daniel Chester French honouring Anderson's generosity was placed near the Carnegie library in Allegheny.
105.explanation: A modest weekly loan of books was repaid on a vast scale by a recipient who never forgot it and who said he resolved to lend books to others if he ever had surplus wealth.
105.tie_back: The kural says the worth of a favour is set by the character of the one who receives it; Anderson's small library became thousands of libraries because of the man who received the kindness.
105._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of the kural's claim that a noble recipient repays far beyond the size of the original help.

106.event_title: The Netherlands' yearly gift of tulips to Canada
106.event: After Germany invaded the Netherlands in 1940, Princess Juliana and her daughters took refuge in Ottawa, where her third daughter Margriet was born in 1943; Canadian troops also played a significant role in liberating the Netherlands in 1945. After returning home, Princess Juliana presented 100,000 tulip bulbs to Canada in gratitude and kept sending bulbs after she became queen. The gift became a lasting tradition, and every year the Dutch royal family and the people of the Netherlands each send 10,000 bulbs to Ottawa.
106.explanation: The gift began as thanks for shelter and liberation in wartime and has been renewed every year for decades, long after the danger passed.
106.tie_back: The kural says never to forsake the friendship of those who stood by you in hard times; the Dutch have kept that friendship alive with tulips every spring since 1945.
106._accuracy_note: A close fit for loyalty to friends who helped in distress, expressed through a renewed national gift rather than a single personal friendship.

107.event_title: Turkey repays Japan for the Ertugrul rescue
107.event: In September 1890 the Ottoman frigate Ertugrul, returning from a goodwill visit to Japan, broke up in a typhoon off the island of Kii Oshima near Kushimoto, and islanders worked through the night to rescue 69 survivors; local physicians later declined Turkey's offer to pay for their care. In March 1985, during the Iran-Iraq War, more than 200 Japanese were stranded in Tehran after Iraq warned it would target aircraft over Iran, and at Japan's request Turkey sent airliners that carried 215 Japanese nationals to safety. When Japan expressed its thanks, Turkish officials cited their nation's debt of gratitude from the Ertugrul rescue 95 years earlier.
107.explanation: A rescue by poor villagers was taught to generations of Turks and repaid almost a century later, when the original rescuers' countrymen were themselves in danger.
107.tie_back: The kural says the good remember through all their births those who wiped away their sorrow; Turkey remembered Kushimoto's kindness across nearly a hundred years and repaid it.
107._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of gratitude remembered across generations; the event is national rather than personal, which suits the kural's hyperbole of seven births.

108.event_title: Pope John Paul II forgives the man who shot him
108.place: Rome, Italy (Gemelli Hospital and a Rome prison)
108.event: On 13 May 1981 Pope John Paul II was shot and seriously wounded in St Peter's Square by Mehmet Ali Agca. Four days later, in a message recorded at the Gemelli hospital and broadcast in St Peter's Square, he said that he was praying for the brother who had shot him, whom he had sincerely forgiven. In 1983 he met Agca in prison and offered him forgiveness in person.
108.explanation: The Pope declared his forgiveness within days, while still recovering from his wounds, rather than waiting for the trial or for time to soften the injury.
108.tie_back: The kural says it is good to let go of a wrong on the very day it is done; John Paul II released the gravest of injuries almost at once.
108._accuracy_note: A strong fit for releasing an injury immediately; the kural also pairs this with remembering benefits, which this event does not illustrate.

109.event_title: Akbar pardons his former regent Bairam Khan
109.event: Bairam Khan, a general and friend of Emperor Humayun, guided the young Akbar as regent after he inherited the throne at the age of 13 in 1556. In 1560 Akbar took the government into his own hands, and Bairam rebelled for a time before submitting; Akbar forgave him and offered him the choice of a high place in the army or an escort for a pilgrimage to Mecca, and Bairam chose the pilgrimage. Bairam was killed by Afghans on the way in 1561, and Akbar took his four-year-old son Abd ur-Rahim into his household; the boy grew up to reach the highest rank in the Mughal hierarchy.
109.explanation: Akbar treated a rebel who had once secured his throne with mercy and later raised the rebel's orphaned son, rather than letting the rebellion cancel the earlier service.
109.tie_back: The kural says even a grievous injury from a former benefactor fades when one remembers the good he once did; Akbar's pardon of Bairam Khan shows past service outweighing present offence.
109._accuracy_note: A good fit, though the sources record the pardon and its terms rather than Akbar's own reasons for showing mercy.

110.event_title: Brutus joins the conspiracy against Julius Caesar
110.event: Marcus Junius Brutus fought on Pompey's side against Julius Caesar, but after Pompey's defeat at Pharsalus in 48 BCE Caesar pardoned him, made him a highly honoured companion, and later put him in charge of Cisalpine Gaul and gave him high civic office. In 44 BCE Brutus joined Cassius and other conspirators in assassinating Caesar in Rome. In the Inferno, written in the early fourteenth century, Dante placed Brutus and Cassius, as betrayers of their benefactor, beside Judas in the lowest region of Hell.
110.explanation: For centuries Brutus's name became shorthand for betrayal of a benefactor, and Dante gave him the harshest place in his entire vision of punishment.
110.tie_back: The kural says there is no escape for one who destroys gratitude for a kindness received; Dante's verdict on Brutus expresses the same judgment in literary form.
110._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of ingratitude condemned without mercy, though Brutus's motives were political and Roman writers judged him in different ways.
